How many watts does a 1,000 W microwave actually use?

Power basics Updated 2026-08-08

More than the number on the door, by roughly a quarter to a half. That figure is COOKING OUTPUT — how much microwave energy reaches the food — and the wall sees the input, which is larger by whatever the magnetron and its transformer lose. The record in this library draws 1,480 W at the socket.

The second surprise is the power-level dial. A conventional microwave has one output level and fakes the rest by switching the magnetron on and off, so a lower setting is a duty cycle rather than a smaller draw. The peak the inverter has to carry is the same on every setting.

Two watt figures, and the label shows the smaller one

What two makers state for the same appliance

Both figures are rating-plate input power, taken from the makers’ own manuals rather than from a review. Neither is the number on the door, and the gap between input and output is not a fixed percentage — it depends on the machine rather than on its size.

Microwave — input power 1,480 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

The rating plate on a countertop machine, which is the figure the door does not show. This is what the inverter carries while the magnetron is conducting.

Microwave — a second maker’s input 1,550 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

A different brand, a LOWER cooking output, and a higher input figure. Whatever else the number on the door tells you, it does not rank machines by what they draw.

Microwave — start-up multiple Not found in the sources we checked no figure to date

The empty row is why this site states no verdict for this appliance, and it is the honest reason rather than an oversight.

A high-voltage transformer has a real switch-on inrush. We have found no published figure for it across the Panasonic, Toshiba and GE documents this record cites, and this library declines to invent a multiple for a load class where the invented number would decide the answer.

Microwave — duty cycle on High 1 Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

Full power on a conventional machine: the magnetron conducts continuously, so the draw above is also the average.

Microwave — duty cycle on power level 7 0.7 Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

The appliance maker’s own words for what the dial does: microwave energy seven-tenths of the time. Same peak, less of it.

Microwave — duty cycle on power level 3 0.3 Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence

And the same again at the bottom of the dial. Defrosting does not ask less of an inverter; it asks the same thing less often.

Electric kettle — running 1,500 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-07 · high confidence

A load in the same room that this site does publish verdicts for, because it is purely resistive and has nothing to inrush.

See the record →

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · microwave oven record · US 120 V

The ratio between the two figures is the part that surprises people who look it up carefully. Our record’s primary source states 1,480 W in for 1,200 W of cooking power, and its cross-check states 1,550 W in for 1,100 W out. That is 1.23× on one machine and 1.41× on the other. A rule of thumb that adds a fixed percentage to the door figure will be wrong on one of them.

A power level is a duty cycle

This is the best household demonstration of the quantity every runtime on this site is computed from. A conventional microwave cannot produce 700 W of cooking energy — it produces its one output level, or nothing, and alternates between the two. The appliance maker cited on this record puts it plainly: power level seven is microwave energy seventy per cent of the time. So the peak an inverter has to carry is identical at every setting, and only the watt-hours change: 1,480 W for the whole of a High cycle, and the same 1,480 W for 0.3 of a defrost cycle.

Why this site publishes no verdict for it

The record is complete enough to quote and not complete enough to judge

Every figure above carries a manufacturer source and a date. What is missing is the start-up demand, and for this class of load that single gap is decisive: a microwave is not a purely resistive appliance — it has a turntable motor, a cooling fan and a large high-voltage transformer — and a verdict computed from running watts alone would tell somebody a machine carries it when the transformer’s switch-on might trip the inverter. So the record is gated. It has no appliance page here, it appears in no ranked list, and no pairing on this site returns a verdict for it. That is a deliberate refusal rather than a missing feature, and it is the same call this library made on a gas furnace blower and on a box fan.

Set that against the kettle in the table above. It draws 1,500 W on the same kind of circuit, which is more than the microwave, and this site ranks every machine against it without hesitation — because a heating element has no inrush to find. The difference between the two is not size and not danger. It is that one of them has a number we could not find, and it happens to be the number that decides the answer.

What to do with your own microwave

Three steps, and the first one is the one most people skip.

1
Read the plate, not the door

The input figure is on the rating label at the back or inside the door frame, usually beside the current draw. On a US machine it will be stated at 120 V.

2
Size on that figure, plus room for a start you cannot see

Since neither the makers nor this library can tell you the inrush, the honest approach is headroom on the continuous rating rather than a number that looks precise.

Open the source →
3
Count watt-hours by setting, not by dial position

Two minutes on High and four minutes at half power cost about the same energy, and ask the inverter for exactly the same peak.

Open the source →

Questions people ask

How many watts does a 1,000 W microwave use?
More than 1,000 W. The figure on the door is cooking output; the input is what the wall and an inverter see. The two records this library cites state 1,480 W in for 1,200 W out and 1,550 W in for 1,100 W out — so the mark-up is somewhere between about a quarter and a half, and it varies by machine rather than by size.
Does a lower power level make a microwave draw fewer watts?
On a conventional machine, no. It produces one output level and cycles the magnetron on and off to average it down, which the appliance maker cited on our record states outright: power level seven is microwave energy seventy per cent of the time. The peak draw is identical at every setting; only the watt-hours fall. Inverter-type microwaves genuinely modulate, and this library holds no record of one.
Will a power station run a microwave?
This site does not answer that one, and the reason is on this page. We have found no published start-up figure for a microwave from any maker in our sources, and a verdict computed from running watts alone could call a machine a pass that would trip when the high-voltage transformer switches on. So the record is quoted here and judged nowhere — no appliance page, no ranked list, no pairing verdict.
